records.title: Healing the cornea: Exploring the therapeutic solutions offered by MSCs and MSC-derived EVs.
records.publisher: Progress in retinal and eye research

content.title: Healing the cornea: Exploring the therapeutic solutions offered by MSCs and MSC-derived EVs.
content.abstract: Affecting a large proportion of the population worldwide, corneal disorders constitute a concerning health hazard associated to compromised eyesight or blindness for most severe cases. In the last decades, mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (MSCs) demonstrated promising abilities in improving symptoms associated to corneal diseases or alleviating these affections, especially through their anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory and pro-regenerative properties. More recently, MSC therapeutic potential was shown to be mediated by the molecules they release, and particularly by their extracellular vesicles (EVs; MSC-EVs). Consequently, using MSC-EVs emerged as a pioneering strategy to mitigate the risks related to cell therapy while providing MSC therapeutic benefits. Despite the promises given by MSC- and MSC-EV-based approaches, many improvements are considered to optimize the therapeutic significance of these therapies. This review aspires to provide a comprehensive and detailed overview of current knowledge on corneal therapies involving MSCs and MSC-EVs, the strategies currently under evaluation, and the gaps remaining to be addressed for clinical implementation. From encapsulating MSCs or their EVs into biomaterials to enhance the ocular retention time to loading MSC-EVs with therapeutic drugs, a wide range of ground-breaking strategies are currently contemplated to lead to the safest and most effective treatments. Promising research initiatives also include diverse gene therapies and the targeting of specific cell types through the modification of the EV surface, paving the way for future therapeutic innovations. As one of the most important challenges, MSC-EV large-scale production strategies are extensively investigated and offer a wide array of possibilities to meet the needs of clinical applications.

records.title: Current Practices, Evolving Techniques, and Immunologic Challenges in Living and Deceased Donor Limbal Stem Cell Transplantation.

content.title: Current Practices, Evolving Techniques, and Immunologic Challenges in Living and Deceased Donor Limbal Stem Cell Transplantation.
content.abstract: This review focuses on allogeneic sources for restoring the ocular surface using limbal stem cell transplantation. We outline the current practices, evolving techniques, and immunologic challenges in living-related and deceased donor limbal stem cell transplantation. The diagnosis and staging guidelines for limbal stem cell deficiency are reviewed. We also explore the currently available treatment approaches, including the Cincinnati protocol for donor/recipient selection criteria and systemic immunosuppression (SI) regimen. Utilization of panel reactive antibody, HLA typing, ABO typing, and donor specific antibodies are highlighted. The traditional techniques as well as more novel variations are described. The importance of 3-agent SI protocols and patient adherence are emphasized to ensure excellent long-term outcomes. The primary immunologic challenge of allogeneic limbal stem cell transplantation, rejection, is also discussed in detail with recommended treatments, including a newer role for intravenous immunoglobulin. Other evolving practices have included a greater reliance on living-related conjunctival limbal allograft over deceased donor keratolimbal allograft due to improved outcomes, decreasing SI in older populations, and lengthening SI regimens due to the possibility of late acute rejection. Finally, we discuss the future of restoring the ocular surface via cell-based therapies, which may have the potential to decrease rejection.

records.title: Pathological mechanism in Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy and myotonic dystrophy type 1: more than meets the eye.
records.publisher: Progress in retinal and eye research

content.title: Pathological mechanism in Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy and myotonic dystrophy type 1: more than meets the eye.
content.abstract: Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy (FECD) is a heritable disorder distinguished by a progressive degeneration of the corneal endothelium. In its late-onset form, FECD has been associated with a trinucleotide repeat (TNR) expansion (CTG18.1) located in an intronic region of the TCF4 gene, whose frequency is variable among different ancestry groups. Since its discovery, studies investigating CTG18.1-mediated pathogenesis have steadily increased, yet much concerning the unique and tissue-specific clinical features of the disease, as well as its heritable mode of transmission, remain poorly understood. The field of repeat expansion disorders has greatly informed mechanistic understanding of CTG18.1-mediated FECD. In particular, molecular mechanisms underlying myotonic dystrophy type 1, attributed to a CTG expansion in the 3' UTR of the DMPK gene, have considerably informed the FECD field, despite its stark contrast in terms of multisystemic manifestations and variable age at onset. In this work, we critically discuss the non-mutually shared pathogenic parallelisms existing between the pathologies, as well as the unique molecular signatures exhibited by FECD and DM1, speculating on potential research directions for future investigations. Moreover, we discuss the few studies published over the past decade describing the occurrence of FECD in DM1 patients. Here, we debate possible shared molecular signatures that could explain FECD development as a consequence of a non-coding CTG expansion, irrespective of loci (e.g. DMPK or TCF4), and discuss experimental approaches to explain whether these pathologies share toxic mechanisms that arise from these distinct repeat elements.

records.title: Seeing anew: Mechanisms, outcomes, and challenges in adapting to restored sight via visual prostheses.
records.publisher: Progress in retinal and eye research

content.title: Seeing anew: Mechanisms, outcomes, and challenges in adapting to restored sight via visual prostheses.
content.abstract: Restoring vision through prosthetic devices represents one of the most ambitious frontiers in translational neuroscience. Despite decades of progress, functional outcomes remain highly variable, often falling short of patient expectations, as adapting to restored vision through visual prostheses is a complex process influenced by neural plasticity, perceptual learning, and psychological factors. We propose a five-stage framework that captures the hierarchically dependent yet fragile process of adaptation: Device Activation, Perceptual Calibration, Cognitive Integration, Behavioral Generalization, and Psychosocial Adjustment. Across retinal and cortical prosthesis designs, the earlier stages are frequently achieved, but progression to fluent, real-world use and sustained device acceptance is far less common. The most consistent point of failure lies between Cognitive Integration and Behavioral Generalization: skills acquired in structured training rarely transfer to unconstrained everyday behavior. Technical constraints, insufficient training, and unrealistic expectations frequently stall adaptation at this threshold, leading to frustration, limited daily use, or device abandonment. By examining visual-prosthesis clinical trials, case studies of surgical vision restoration, and evidence from cochlear implants and sensory substitution devices, we identify key determinants of successful adaptation: timely intervention, intuitive device usability, sustained rehabilitation, and long-term psychosocial support. Understanding the mechanisms of adaptation is essential for improving visual prostheses and ultimately enhancing quality of life for individuals with restored sight.

records.title: Cytopathology and Prognostic Accuracy of 15-GEP/PRAME: The Collaborative Ocular Oncology Group Study 2.

content.title: Cytopathology and Prognostic Accuracy of 15-GEP/PRAME: The Collaborative Ocular Oncology Group Study 2.
content.abstract:
Importance

Gene expression profiling (GEP) reliably predicts metastatic uveal melanoma risk and is used to manage uveal melanoma (UM) in patients with this diagnosis. Efforts to refine molecular prognostication continue.

Objective

To determine if confirmatory cytopathology findings influence the prognostic accuracy of a commercially available GEP/Preferentially Expressed Antigen in Melanoma (PRAME) assay.

Design, setting, and participants

The Collaborative Ocular Oncology Group 2 study, a prospective cohort study, was conducted from 2017 to 2020 with follow-up recorded at 6-month intervals. This was a multicenter study that included patients with choroidal and/or ciliary body melanoma and results from a 15-GEP and PRAME RNA expression (15-GEP/PRAME) assay. Patients with iris tumors or less than 6 months' follow-up were excluded. Study data were analyzed from April 2025 to July 2026.

Exposures

15-GEP/PRAME, cytopathology, and next-generation sequencing (NGS).

Main outcomes and measures

Metastatic uveal melanoma rates in patients who had 15-GEP/PRAME and confirmatory cytopathology (CCP) results confirming or suspicious for UM (GEP+CCP) were compared with those who had 15-GEP/PRAME and no cytopathology performed, or unknown or nondiagnostic cytopathology results (GEP only). UM-associated variants identified by NGS were also evaluated.

Results

Of 1537 patients (mean [SD] age, 62.0 [13.4] years; 787 male [51.2%]), 727 (47.3%) had CCP results, and 810 (52.7%) had nondiagnostic cytopathology results or no cytopathology performed. Class 2/PRAME+ tumors were more common (136 of 727 [18.7%]) in the GEP+CCP group than in the GEP-only group (72 of 810 [8.9%]; 9.8% difference; 95% CI, 6.4-13.3; P <.001), whereas class 1/PRAME- tumors were less common (330 of 727 [45.4%] vs 495 of 810 [61.1%]; 15.7% difference; 95% CI, 10.8-20.6; P <.001). In patients with GEP+CCP, 22.7% (n = 165) developed metastasis vs 15.4% (n = 125) in patients with GEP only (7.3% difference, 95% CI, 3.3-11.2; P < .001). Adjusting for 15-GEP/PRAME status, there were no differences in metastasis rates between CCP groups. Of 1327 patients with successful NGS, 94.1% (605 of 643) in the GEP+CCP group and 71.9% (492 of 684) in the GEP-only group had a UM-associated variant (22.2% difference, 95% CI, 18.3-26.0; P < .001).

Conclusions and relevance

Results of this cohort study reveal that no differences in metastasis outcomes were observed between patients with and without CCP within any GEP/PRAME categories. UM-associated variants were found less frequently in the GEP-only group than in the GEP+CCP group. In this cohort, 15-GEP/PRAME classification without CCP retained prognostic validity, supporting its clinical consideration in guiding metastatic surveillance in cases in which cytopathology is unavailable.

records.title: Longitudinal Changes in Scleral Thickness after Half-dose Photodynamic Therapy in Central Serous Chorioretinopathy.

content.title: Longitudinal Changes in Scleral Thickness after Half-dose Photodynamic Therapy in Central Serous Chorioretinopathy.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To evaluate longitudinal changes in scleral thickness after half-dose photodynamic therapy (PDT) in eyes with central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC) in parallel with widefield assessment of choroidal thickness.

Methods

This retrospective observational study included 41 eyes of 41 patients with unilateral CSC who underwent half-dose PDT for persistent subretinal fluid and completed 12 months of follow-up. Scleral thickness was measured in 4 quadrants using anterior-segment optical coherence tomography (OCT) at baseline and at 3 and 12 months after PDT. Widefield choroidal thickness was assessed using widefield swept-source OCT with an 18-mm grid divided into 9 sectors. Untreated fellow eyes served as a reference group.

Results

In treated eyes, widefield choroidal thickness decreased significantly at 3 months after PDT across all 9 predefined sectors (all P < 0.05) and remained reduced at 12 months, with no significant differences between 3 and 12 months. In untreated fellow eyes, no consistent longitudinal changes in choroidal thickness were observed; however, a statistically significant reduction was noted only in the outer superonasal sector at 3 months (P = 0.015). In contrast, scleral thickness showed no significant changes at any time point in either treated or fellow eyes (all P > 0.05).

Conclusions

Despite widespread and sustained choroidal thinning after half-dose PDT, scleral thickness remained unchanged for at least 12 months in eyes with CSC. These findings suggest that scleral thickening in CSC is unlikely to represent a readily reversible response to treatment-associated choroidal changes and may instead reflect a relatively stable anatomical feature.

records.title: A Comprehensive Meta-Analysis on the Role of Analgesics and Anti-Inflammatories in Pan-Retinal Photocoagulation.

content.title: A Comprehensive Meta-Analysis on the Role of Analgesics and Anti-Inflammatories in Pan-Retinal Photocoagulation.
content.abstract:
Purpose

Pan-retinal photocoagulation (PRP) is the mainstay of treatment for proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), reducing the risk of severe vision loss. Pain poses a potential obstacle to effective laser delivery and patient compliance. Therefore, implementing pain relief strategies can enhance both treatment efficacy and patient comfort.

Design

A systematic review and meta-analysis.

Methods

We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis according to PRISMA guidelines. The PubMed, Embase and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials databases were searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that enrolled patients undergoing PRP due to DR and compared analgesics or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAID) to placebo. Pain was evaluated with the visual analogue scale. The version 2 of the Cochrane Collaboration's Risk of Bias in Randomized Controlled Trials tool and its version for crossover trials were used to assess the risk of bias. The Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation tool was used to measure the certainty of evidence.

Results

A total of 13 studies were included, comprising 1404 eyes from RCTs, nine of which were crossover. Patients who were administered analgesia reported a significantly lower pain sensitivity compared to those who received placebo (Standardized mean difference [SMD] -0.38; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.58, -0.17; P < .01; I2 = 69%). Subgroup analysis of systemic administration of analgesics/NSAIDs (metamizole, Entonox, acetaminophen, ibuprofen, caffeine, mefenamic acid, intramuscular ketorolac tromethamine, and potassium diclofenac) also showed a statistically significant reduction in pain when compared to placebo (SMD -0.28; 95% CI -0.50, -0.07; P < .01; I2 = 43%). Exclusive eye drops administration (ketorolac tromethamine 0.5% and sodium diclofenac 0.1%) also showed a significant difference in pain sensitivity (SMD -0.46; 95% CI -0.88, -0.05; I2 = 83%), however with a more significant heterogeneity.

Conclusions

The results of this meta-analysis including over 1000 patients demonstrated that the use of analgesics significantly reduced pain sensitivity during PRP, and systemic analgesia is potentially better than topical administration when compared to placebo.

records.title: Novel insights into retinoblastoma: From oncogenic circuitry to precision diagnosis and eye-preserving therapies.
records.publisher: Progress in retinal and eye research

content.title: Novel insights into retinoblastoma: From oncogenic circuitry to precision diagnosis and eye-preserving therapies.
content.abstract: Retinoblastoma (RB) represents the most common primary intraocular malignancy in childhood and stands as a paradigm for translating molecular oncology into precision clinical management. This review synthesizes the comprehensive evolution in the understanding and treatment of RB. First, we deconstruct the intricate oncogenic circuitry that extends far beyond Knudson's classic "two-hit" RB1 inactivation model, describing non-classical MYCN-driven pathogenesis, multi-layered epigenetic reprogramming (including chromatin, RNA and histone changes), and distinct histological subtypes with defined clinical correlates, such as the favorable-prognosis cavitary RB. Single-cell genomics has elucidated the cellular origin from cone precursor cells and intratumoral heterogeneity. Risk stratification has been refined through well-defined classification systems, from the therapy-guiding International Intraocular Retinoblastoma Classification (IIRC) to the comprehensive American Joint Committee on Cancer Tumor-Node-metastasis (AJCC TNM) staging. Furthermore, the diagnostic paradigm has advanced from conventional anatomical imaging to liquid biopsies, enabling non-invasive molecular staging and monitoring via tumor-derived cell-free DNA analysis. Concurrently, the therapeutic landscape has undergone a radical shift, moving from enucleation and external-beam radiotherapy to an era dominated by local sight-preserving strategies. We provide a critical synthesis of the evidence for intravenous chemotherapy and the transformative role of super-selective intra-arterial chemotherapy (IAC), and describe essential randomized controlled trials, technical innovations, and optimized drug regimens. Finally, we explore emerging targeted molecular therapies and future directions. By integrating cutting-edge molecular insights with robust, high-level clinical evidence, this review offers the framework for achieving patient and eye survival as well as vision preservation in children with Retinoblastoma.

records.title: Progression Rate of Macular Retinal Pigment Epithelium Atrophy in Geographic Atrophy and Selected Inherited Retinal Dystrophies. A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

content.title: Progression Rate of Macular Retinal Pigment Epithelium Atrophy in Geographic Atrophy and Selected Inherited Retinal Dystrophies. A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To compare the macular retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) atrophy progression rate of selected degenerative and macular inherited retinal diseases (IRD).

Design

Systematic review and meta-analysis.

Methods

The protocol was registered on the PROSPERO database. Medline, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Google Scholar were searched up to September 15, 2023 for articles reporting the RPE atrophy growth rate in treatment-naïve eyes with geographic atrophy (GA), Stargardt disease (STGD1), Best disease, pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE), central areolar choroidal dystrophy (CACD), or pattern dystrophies with no previous or current macular neovascularization and a minimum follow-up time of 12 months. Meta-analyses determined mean RPE atrophy growth rates per disease, imaging modality (fundus autofluorescence [FAF], optical coherence tomography [OCT], or color fundus photography [CFP]) and metric (mm2/y or mm/y). The Newcastle-Ottawa scale and the Cochrane Risk-of-Bias tool assessed the risk of bias, and funnel plots were used to evaluate small-study effects.

Results

From 4354 publications, 85 were included for meta-analysis: 69 studies (7815 eyes) on GA, 15 (1367 eyes) on STGD1, and one on both. Two studies on PXE were only eligible for review. No studies for other diseases met our eligibility criteria. The overall mean RPE atrophy growth rate for GA using FAF was 1.65 mm2/y (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.49-1.81) and 0.35 mm/y (95% CI, 0.28-0.41); using OCT, it was 1.46 mm2/y (95% CI, 1.28-1.64) and 0.34 mm/y (95% CI, 0.28-0.40); and on CFP it was 1.76 mm2/y (95% CI, 1.56-1.97) and 0.30 mm/y (95% CI, 0.28-0.31). For STGD1, using FAF it was 1.0 mm2/y (95% CI, 0.77-1.23) and 0.20 mm/y (95% CI, 0.17-0.23); on OCT, it was 0.80 mm2/y (95% CI, 0.72-0.88). No studies on STGD1 reported the growth rate with other imaging modalities or metrics. Growth rates in GA were faster than in STGD1 (p < .05). A larger baseline area of atrophy was generally associated with faster growth rates.

Conclusions

The RPE atrophy growth rate in GA is faster than in STGD1 but with great variation between studies and imaging modalities. Limited information was available for other macular IRD, suggesting further research is needed.

records.title: Efficacy of Customized Photorefractive Keratectomy With Cross-Linking Versus Cross-Linking Alone in Progressive Keratoconus: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

content.title: Efficacy of Customized Photorefractive Keratectomy With Cross-Linking Versus Cross-Linking Alone in Progressive Keratoconus: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Topic

This review evaluates the effectiveness and safety of combining cPRK with CXL versus CXL alone in improving visual outcomes for patients with progressive keratoconus.

Design

Systematic review and meta-analysis.

Clinical relevance

Keratoconus leads to vision loss and affects quality of life. While CXL is the current standard for halting progression, it does not correct the visual impairment. This review explores whether adding cPRK to CXL offers better visual outcomes while maintaining the same safety, potentially refining treatment approaches.

Methods

A systematic search of MEDLINE, PubMed, Cochrane Library and EMBASE was conducted through September 2024, following PRISMA guidelines. The initial study design aimed to include randomized controlled trials (RCTs) as well as comparative nonrandomized prospective or retrospective studies evaluating CXL+cPRK versus CXL alone, with a minimum follow-up of six months. However, only nonrandomized studies were retrieved. As a result, all included studies were assessed for the risk of bias using the ROBINS-I tool. The primary outcomes were uncorrected distance visual acuity (UDVA) and corrected distance visual acuity (CDVA). Secondary outcomes included refraction, corneal structure, and higher-order aberrations (HOA). Meta-analysis was performed using standardized mean differences (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), and heterogeneity was assessed using a random-effects model where necessary. Sensitivity analysis was conducted using a leave-one-out approach to assess the robustness of the results. This study is registered in the PROSPERO database (CRD42024594757).

Results

Eight nonrandomized studies involving 731 eyes from 706 patients were analyzed. Compared to CXL alone, the combination of CXL+cPRK significantly improved postoperative UDVA (SMD = -0.39, 95% CI: -0.69 to -0.08, P = .01) and CDVA (SMD = -0.57, 95% CI: -0.96 to -0.18, P = .004), while also reducing refractive cylinder error. Additionally, CXL+cPRK led to reductions in coma, total HOA, coma-like aberrations, mean keratometry (KM), and central corneal thickness (CCT). No significant differences were observed between the groups in endothelial cell count (ECC). The rate of postoperative ectasia progression was comparable between both groups. All included studies exhibited at least one ROBINS-I domain at high risk of bias, particularly related to confounding. The heterogeneity observed in this analysis was primarily attributed to differences in surgical techniques, patient selection criteria, and study designs across the included studies.

Conclusions

Customized PRK combined with CXL provides superior postoperative visual acuity (UDVA, CDVA) and visual quality compared to CXL alone while maintaining the same corneal stability in the management of progressive keratoconus. Only nonrandomized studies could be retrieved for the purpose of the study.

records.title: SURGICAL DRAINAGE METHODS DURING PARS PLANA VITRECTOMY FOR RHEGMATOGENOUS RETINAL DETACHMENT: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

content.title: SURGICAL DRAINAGE METHODS DURING PARS PLANA VITRECTOMY FOR RHEGMATOGENOUS RETINAL DETACHMENT: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To assess efficacy and safety outcomes of subretinal fluid drainage methods during pars plana vitrectomy for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.

Methods

A systematic search strategy was conducted for studies published between January 2000 and October 2022. Included studies reported on either the safety or efficacy of two or more drainage methods during pars plana vitrectomy for patients with rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.

Results

Two randomized and five observational studies consisting of 1,524 eyes were included. Best-corrected visual acuity at the last study observation and primary reattachment rates were similar across groups. A significantly lower risk of epiretinal membrane formation was associated with draining subretinal fluid through preexisting retinal breaks (risk ratio = 0.70, 95% confidence interval = [0.60, 0.83], P = <0.01, I 2 = 0%) or with perfluorocarbon liquid (risk ratios = 0.70, 95% confidence interval = [0.59, 0.83], P = <0.01, I 2 = 0%) compared with posterior retinotomy. The risk of an abnormal foveal contour was significantly greater in perfluorocarbon liquid-treated eyes relative to posterior retinotomy (risk ratios = 1.56, 95% confidence interval = [1.13, 2.17], P = <0.01, I 2 = 0%).

Conclusion

No significant differences were observed in the final best-corrected visual acuity at the last study observation and primary reattachment rates across different drainage methods. There remains limited information on the topic, so future research is warranted.

records.title: Effectiveness and Safety of Trabeculectomy Versus Tube Shunt Implantation for Uveitic Glaucoma: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

content.title: Effectiveness and Safety of Trabeculectomy Versus Tube Shunt Implantation for Uveitic Glaucoma: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To evaluate the effectiveness and safety of trabeculectomy compared to glaucoma drainage devices (GDDs) in managing uveitic glaucoma (UG).

Design

Systematic review.

Methods

We searched seven electronic databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, EMBASE, CENTRAL, and Google Scholar) to compare trabeculectomy with various GDDs in UG. The primary outcome was intraocular pressure (IOP) reduction, and secondary outcomes included postoperative complications. We fitted a random effects model for meta-analysis and assessed the risk of bias using the National Institute of Health quality assessment tool.

Results

We included eight studies; 197 eyes underwent trabeculectomy, and 277 eyes had GDDs. The mean age of participants was 48.5 years, with ∼53.5% being male in the trabeculectomy group and 49.3% in the GDDs group. The meta-analysis revealed no significant difference in IOP reduction between trabeculectomy and GDDs (P = .48). Subgroup analyses revealed no significant difference in IOP reduction between trabeculectomy and either the Ahmed glaucoma drainage device group (P = .38) or the Baerveldt glaucoma implant group (P = .90). GDDs were associated with higher rates of complications such as cystoid macular edema (CME) (15% vs. 4%, P < .001), need for revision surgery (11% vs. 6%, P = .04), and uveitic flare (5% vs. 0%, P = .001). However, trabeculectomy had a higher risk of cataract progression (7% vs. 1%, P < .001).

Conclusion

Trabeculectomy and GDDs demonstrated comparable effectiveness in reducing IOP or glaucoma medication reduction in UG. However, there were significant differences in their safety profiles; CME and revisions were higher in GDD, and cataract progression was higher after trabeculectomy.

records.title: Pars Plana Vitrectomy With Silicone Oil or Gas Tamponade for Uncomplicated Retinal Detachment: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

content.title: Pars Plana Vitrectomy With Silicone Oil or Gas Tamponade for Uncomplicated Retinal Detachment: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To compare the efficacy and safety of pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) with silicone oil compared to gas tamponade for uncomplicated rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD).

Design

Systematic review and meta-analysis.

Methods

A systematic literature search was conducted on Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library from January 2000 to September 2023 for comparative studies evaluating the efficacy and safety of PPV with either silicone oil or gas tamponade in the setting of uncomplicated RRD. Our primary outcome was best-corrected visual acuity at the last study observation. Secondary outcomes included the rates of retinal reattachment, retinal thickness, and the incidence of adverse events. We performed a meta-analysis using a random-effects model.

Results

Nine observational studies reporting on 491 RRD eyes were included. The mean best-corrected visual acuity at the last study observation was significantly better in the gas tamponade group than in the silicone oil group (weighted mean difference [WMD] = 0.17 logMAR, 95% confidence interval [CI] = [0.06, 0.27], P = .002). Rates of primary retinal reattachment were similar between the silicone oil and gas tamponade groups (P = .89). The ganglion cell layer was significantly thinner in the silicone oil group compared to the gas tamponade group (WMD =-3.70 µm, 95% CI = [-5.87, -1.53, P = .0008), as was the inner plexiform layer (WMD = -2.45, 95% CI = [-4.50, -0.40], P = .02) and outer nuclear layer (WMD = -11.74 µm, 95% CI = [-18.39, -5.10], P = .0005).

Conclusions

PPV with gas tamponade was associated with better functional outcomes compared to PPV with silicone oil, although both tamponades yielded comparable primary reattachment rates. The absence of randomized trials and the potential for selection bias underscore the importance of further investigation in diverse patient populations.

records.title: Accuracy of six contemporary toric formulas: analysis of 6753 eyes.
records.publisher: Journal of cataract and refractive surgery

content.title: Accuracy of six contemporary toric formulas: analysis of 6753 eyes.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To compare the predictive accuracy of 4 toric intraocular lens (IOL) formulas (Barrett, EVO, Hoffer QST, and Kane) integrated in the ESCRS calculator. Barrett and EVO were tested with measured (Barrett M and EVO M) and predicted (Barrett P and EVO P) posterior corneal curvature.

Setting

Multiple surgical centers in the United States.

Design

Retrospective database study.

Methods

6753 eyes implanted with nontoric IOLs were analyzed. Preoperative biometry, including posterior corneal curvature, was obtained using the IOLMaster 700. Predicted residual astigmatism was calculated through the proprietary websites of the 4 toric formulas integrated into the ESCRS IOL power calculator. Primary endpoints were the mean vector magnitude error and proportions of eyes with vector magnitude prediction errors ≤0.50 diopters (D).

Results

Kane demonstrated the lowest mean vector magnitude prediction error (0.537 D), significantly lower than EVO P (0.561 D), EVO M (0.57 D), Barrett M (0.579 D), Barrett P (0.583 D), and Hoffer QST (0.622 D) (all P < .001). This result was consistent in with-the-rule, against-the-rule, and oblique subgroups. Kane also achieved the highest proportion of eyes with prediction error ≤0.50 D ( P < .001). For all formulas, centroid values were significantly different from zero. The Kane formula showed the lowest total variances, significantly lower than all other formulas ( P < .001).

Conclusions

The Kane formula showed statistically superior predictive accuracy with the lowest errors and variances and the highest proportion of eyes within 0.50 D. However, differences among formulas were small, and their clinical relevance for toric IOL outcomes remains uncertain.

records.title: Baseline OCT Biomarkers Predicting Visual Outcomes in Neovascular Age-Related Macular Degeneration: A Meta-Analysis.

content.title: Baseline OCT Biomarkers Predicting Visual Outcomes in Neovascular Age-Related Macular Degeneration: A Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Topic

To determine the effect estimates and certainty of evidence for baseline OCT biomarkers predicting visual acuity (VA) and changes in VA from baseline at 6, 12, and 24 months after anti-vascular endothelial growth factor therapy for neovascular age-related macular degeneration.

Clinical relevance

Understanding the prognostic utility of biomarkers can improve treatment decisions.

Methods

Results were reported in ETDRS letters. Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations (GRADE) guidelines for prognostic studies informed certainty of evidence. Results were interpreted using a 5-letter minimally important difference.

Results

Twenty-nine reports (8863 eyes) evaluating 80 biomarkers were included. Two biomarkers predicted better VA at 12 months with a low-certainty: the presence of an intact external limiting membrane (+14.0; 95% confidence interval [CI], +3.1 to +24.8) and the presence of an intact ellipsoid zone (+6.8; 95% CI, +2.8 to +10.8). Three biomarkers predicted worse VA at 12 months with a low certainty; the presence of intraretinal fluid (IRF; -5.6; 95% CI, -9.7 to -1.5), the presence of IRF in the foveal center point (-7.4; 95% CI, -10.1 to -4.7), and the presence of subretinal hyperreflective material (-8.7; 95% CI, -19.0 to 1.6). No other biomarker predicted an effect size that crossed the minimally important difference. However, noteworthy results occurred when interpreting biomarkers with statistically significant findings relative to a threshold of 0 letters and moderate certainty: the presence of a pigment epithelial detachment, geographic atrophy (GA), and both IRF and subretinal fluid (SRF) predicted reduced vision at 12 months. The presence of SRF predicted a positive change in VA at 12 months. The absence of a posterior vitreous detachment predicted a negative change in VA at 12 months. Finally, the presence of IRF in the central 1 mm, retinal pigment epithelial elevation, and GA predicted negative changes in VA at 24 months.

Discussion

With low-certainty evidence, the baseline presence of an intact external limiting membrane and ellipsoid zone predicted better VA at 12 months, and the presence of IRF, IRF in the foveal center point, and subretinal hyperreflective material predicted worse VA at 12 months. Improved standardization in biomarker classification and control of confounding variables is needed.

Financial disclosure(s)

Proprietary or commercial disclosure may be found in the Footnotes and Disclosures at the end of this article.

records.title: Transformation of the extracellular matrix during uveal melanoma development, progression, and at the hepatic metastatic niche.
records.publisher: Progress in retinal and eye research

content.title: Transformation of the extracellular matrix during uveal melanoma development, progression, and at the hepatic metastatic niche.
content.abstract: The tumour microenvironment comprising tumour cells, immune infiltrates, stromal components, and the extracellular matrix (ECM) plays a central role in cancer biology, modulating key hallmarks, such as proliferation, immune evasion, and metastasis. The ECM is a dynamic network of collagens, elastin, glycoproteins, and proteoglycans and emerging evidence highlights its role in tumour progression, with loss of matrix organisation altering tumour cell behaviour through both pro- and anti-tumourigenic mechanisms. Uveal melanoma (UM), the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults, carries a poor prognosis due to its propensity for hepatic metastasis and limited therapeutic options. The uveal tract, comprising the choroid, ciliary body, and iris, relies on highly specialised ECM architectures, and we describe in this review how they support nutrient exchange, lens accommodation, and light regulation while mediating essential biochemical and biomechanical signalling. Understanding this baseline ECM is essential for interpreting the pathological matrix remodelling that occurs in UM. We describe marked compositional differences in ECM between low- and high-metastatic risk primary UM, revealing key mechanisms of tumour progression, including upregulation of structural collagens, fibronectin, laminins, and ECM-remodelling enzymes that activate oncogenic signalling pathways enhancing proliferation, invasion, and metastatic competence. We also explore the hepatic metastatic niche, where stellate cell-driven ECM remodelling promotes a fibrotic, immune-restrictive microenvironment that limits therapeutic efficacy. Finally, we discuss experimental constraints limiting ECM research and highlight advances in decellularised scaffolds, three-dimensional culture systems, and multi-omics technologies to dissect tumour-matrix interactions and uncover ECM-targeted therapeutic vulnerabilities with the potential to improve UM's poor clinical outcomes.

records.title: Assessing the Fragility of Statistically Significant Outcomes in Randomized Controlled Trials of Minimally Invasive Glaucoma Surgery (MIGS).

content.title: Assessing the Fragility of Statistically Significant Outcomes in Randomized Controlled Trials of Minimally Invasive Glaucoma Surgery (MIGS).
content.abstract:
Topic

Minimally invasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS) has been widely adopted as a surgical option for glaucoma, yet concerns remain regarding the robustness of the evidence supporting many procedures. The fragility index (FI) and fragility quotient (FQ) provide complementary measures to traditional p values by quantifying how dependent statistically significant results are on a small number of outcome events.

Clinical relevance

Understanding the statistical fragility of MIGS trials is important for clinicians, guideline developers, and policymakers when interpreting reported efficacy and safety outcomes, particularly in a field characterised by small trials, heterogeneous endpoints, and commercially sensitive interventions.

Methods

A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines and registered on PROSPERO. Electronic databases were searched from inception to August 1, 2025, to identify randomized controlled trials evaluating MIGS procedures in patients with glaucoma. Trials reporting at least one statistically significant binary outcome with sufficient raw data were included. The FI was calculated using iterative Fisher exact testing, and the FQ was derived by normalizing FI to total sample size. Risk of bias was assessed using the Revised Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool (RoB 2.0).

Results

Sixteen randomized controlled trials encompassing 4,562 participants met inclusion criteria. The median sample size was 236.5 (interquartile range [IQR], 88-511), with a median follow-up of 24 months. The mean FI was 9.4 ± 10.0 and the mean FQ was 0.031 ± 0.025, indicating that approximately 3% of participants would require a different outcome to render results non-significant. Three trials (18.8%) had an FI of zero. In six studies (37.5%), the FI was less than or equal to the number of participants lost to follow-up, suggesting vulnerability to attrition bias. Fragility varied across device categories, with larger multicenter trials demonstrating higher FI values but consistently low FQ values.

Conclusion

Statistically significant outcomes in RCTs of MIGS exhibit variable statistical robustness when assessed using fragility metrics, often due to small numbers of events. These findings highlight the need for cautious interpretation of reported significance and support the incorporation of fragility metrics alongside conventional statistical measures when appraising the MIGS evidence base.

records.title: Adherence of Economic Evaluations of Interventions for Retinal Conditions to CHEERS Guidelines: A Systematic Review and Critical Appraisal.

content.title: Adherence of Economic Evaluations of Interventions for Retinal Conditions to CHEERS Guidelines: A Systematic Review and Critical Appraisal.
content.abstract:
Purpose

There have been rapid advancements in treatment of retinal disease, with the recent development of novel therapies for many common conditions. Economic evaluation studies are used to examine the implications of implementing health interventions. The objectives of this review were to (1) assess the reporting quality of economic evaluations on retina-related conditions, and (2) evaluate the risk of bias of identified studies, given the implications of bias on study critical appraisal.

Study design

Systematic review.

Methods

A literature search was conducted using MEDLINE and Embase (OvidSP) and Cochrane (Wiley) to identify relevant studies published between January 1, 2013 and December 17, 2024. Reporting quality was appraised using the 2022 CHEERS checklist and converted to numerical scores to facilitate data analysis. The JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Economic Evaluations was used to assess risk of bias.

Results

A total of 174 studies were included. The average CHEERS checklist compliance was 63%, with no trend of improvement or decline in reporting quality over time. Studies most often failed to report the health economic analysis plan (only 5% of studies reported), effect of and approach to engagement with patients and stakeholders (4% and 11% respectively), distributional effects (6%), and characterization of heterogeneity (33%). Only 5% of studies had a publicly available model.

Conclusions

Gaps exist in reporting population heterogeneity, participation of patient and public stakeholders, and fully transparent study methodology in vitreoretinal ophthalmology economic evaluations. Ophthalmology health economics researchers should consider including these details to ameliorate interpretation and application of study findings.

records.title: ASSOCIATION BETWEEN RETINAL PIGMENT EPITHELIUM TEAR AND ANTI-VASCULAR ENDOTHELIAL GROWTH FACTOR THERAPY: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

content.title: ASSOCIATION BETWEEN RETINAL PIGMENT EPITHELIUM TEAR AND ANTI-VASCULAR ENDOTHELIAL GROWTH FACTOR THERAPY: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To identify the prevalence of retinal pigment epithelium tear (RPET) after anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) therapy and determine the efficacy of continued anti-VEGF therapy in patients with RPET.

Methods

All relevant clinical trials and observational studies in several online databases were screened. The main outcomes were the incidence of RPET after anti-VEGF therapy and changes in visual acuity for patients with RPET treated with continued anti-VEGF.

Results

The pooled incidence of RPET after anti-VEGF therapy from 24 studies with 17,354 patients was 1.9% (95% CI: 1.3-2.7). Most new RPET cases were concentrated in the first month at baseline or after the first injection during anti-VEGF therapy and gradually decreased by the subsequent month or injection. 13 studies with 157 patients reported that for patients who received anti-VEGF therapy after RPET, their pooled best-corrected visual acuity improved, but did not reach a significant level (standardized mean differences 0.34; 95% CI: -0.03 to 0.71).

Conclusion

The incidence of RPET after anti-VEGF therapy is low. The intravitreal anti-VEGF injection may accelerate this process. For patients with RPET, maintenance of anti-VEGF therapy ensures visual acuity stability.

records.title: Comparison of refractive surgeries (SMILE, LASIK, and PRK) with and without corneal crosslinking: systematic review and meta-analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of cataract and refractive surgery

content.title: Comparison of refractive surgeries (SMILE, LASIK, and PRK) with and without corneal crosslinking: systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract: Corneal crosslinking (CXL) is used for treating keratoconus and post-laser in situ keratomileusis ectasia. However, refractive surgery is not usually performed with prophylactic CXL. Therefore, we performed a meta-analysis comparing outcomes of refractive surgeries with vs without prophylactic CXL. We systematically searched databases for studies comparing refractive surgeries for myopic correction with vs without prophylactic corneal crosslinking. Review Manager 5.4.1 was used to perform statistical analysis. We included 2820 eyes from 28 studies. Compared with refractive surgery alone, surgery with prophylactic CXL resulted in decreased central corneal thickness, corrected distance visual acuity logMAR, and safety and efficacy indices. There were no significant differences in postoperative uncorrected distance visual acuity of 20/20 or better at ≥12 months and other visual outcomes among both groups. More randomized controlled trials with standard crosslinking protocols are needed to analyze the prophylactic use of crosslinking with refractive surgeries.

records.title: An Agentic AI Workflow for Automated Macular Hole Diagnosis and Structured Report Generation.

content.title: An Agentic AI Workflow for Automated Macular Hole Diagnosis and Structured Report Generation.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Current AI models for optical coherence tomography (OCT) primarily focus on diagnosis as a standalone task. We developed and validated an end-to-end agentic AI workflow that integrates automated macular hole (MH) diagnosis from OCT images with structured patient-friendly report generation.

Methods

The proposed sequential workflow coordinated by a workflow orchestration agent consisted of an image diagnosis stage and a language generation step. The OCT version of RETFound, a self-supervised retinal foundation model, was fine-tuned for binary classification of macular OCT scans as MH or normal macula. Training, validation, and internal testing were performed using multiple public OCT datasets with patient-level stratified splitting, followed by external validation on two independent datasets. The performance of the fine-tuned foundation model was evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC). For each new OCT image, the AI agent used the trained RETFound model to classify the image, received the diagnostic output, incorporated it into a structured prompt, and called the large language model (GPT-4) to generate the clinical report.

Results

On the internal test set (n = 180), the model achieved an accuracy of 100% (95% confidence interval (CI), 97.9-100%) with an AUC of 1.00. On external validation (n = 1014), accuracy was 98.8% (95% CI 97.9-99.3%), sensitivity was 97.9% (95% CI 96.3-98.8%), specificity was 100% (95% CI 99.2-100.0%), and AUC was 0.999 (95% CI 0.998-1.000). Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) analysis showed that predictions were driven by relevant retinal regions, particularly the macular hole and adjacent layers. The end-to-end agentic AI workflow generated concise and standardized patient-friendly reports for all samples, without the language model influencing diagnostic decisions.

Conclusions

This study demonstrates the feasibility of an end-to-end AI workflow coordinated by a workflow orchestration agent for robust OCT-based MH diagnosis with a large language model for structured report generation. By separating image-based diagnosis from language generation, this approach offers a practical and scalable solution for virtual vitreoretinal clinics.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Laser-Assisted Refractive Surgery-A Comprehensive Review.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Laser-Assisted Refractive Surgery-A Comprehensive Review.
content.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology-in the form of Machine Learning (ML) models and other models specialized in image recognition and processing, such as Convolutional Neural Networks Visual Transformers (CNN-ViTs)-is increasingly being used in ophthalmology. This review summarizes the main AI applications for laser-assisted refractive surgery. Methods: A wide-ranging literature search on the PubMed and ISI Thompson Web of Science databases was conducted. Results: AI is an all-encompassing technological concept that refers to either specific applications of ML/CNN models, such as in keratoconus screening or diagnosis, or agentic/multimodal AI applications that process different data types using a variety of AI models. The most clinically established applications found were corneal ectasia and keratoconus screening, in which AI models can reliably exceed 95% diagnostic accuracy, specificity, and sensitivity; nomogram-derived laser ablation programming; optimization of ray-tracing calculations for ray-traced ablation profiles; patient screening and selection for refractive surgery; visual and refractive result prediction; assessment of postoperative corneal ectasia risk; detection of intraoperative complications; research on the laser coupling effect; and other applications such as monitoring eye rubbing behavior in corneal ectasia suspects. Thus, singular, specific applications of AI models have made the largest clinical contributions. These results must be interpreted with a comparison of internal versus external validation, calibration, and generalizability. Overall the technology is highly promising. Agentic/multimodal AI frameworks are currently being discussed, with pilot studies published and applicability proposed in the context of large, high-patient-volume clinical practices. The technological advent of SHAP force plot graphs and saliency maps has improved understanding of the factors that contribute mechanistically to AI model reasoning, leading to more informed clinical decisions or research applicability, such as in finding parameters or factors linked to postoperative ectasia. Conclusions: AI is already established in laser-assisted refractive surgery in the form of models specialized in data-intensive analysis. At present, the best-performing novel AI models originate from the domain of large or multi-hospital settings due to requirements for multiple latest-generation diagnostic devices, high-volume patient data, computing expertise, and resources. Future directions could include clinical standardization and trickle-down dissemination of the technology. Agentic/multimodal AI has the potential to benefit large clinical/patient settings or offer access to expert knowledge in smaller practice settings. Agentic/multimodal AI implementation is offset by challenges in complexity, the technological limitations of LLMs ("hallucinations"), and ethical and legislative factors.

records.title: Retinal Artificial Intelligence Reclassifies SCORE2-Based Cardiovascular Risk Across the ESC/EAS Statin-Indication Boundary: A UK Biobank Prospective Cohort Study.

content.title: Retinal Artificial Intelligence Reclassifies SCORE2-Based Cardiovascular Risk Across the ESC/EAS Statin-Indication Boundary: A UK Biobank Prospective Cohort Study.
content.abstract:
Aims

Whether a retinal artificial intelligence (AI) risk score reclassifies SCORE2 cardiovascular risk stratification in statin-naive adults across the ESC/EAS statin-indication boundary is uncertain. We evaluated the retinal AI risk score for 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) prediction.

Methods

In 40,672 statin-naive UK Biobank participants (aged 40-69, without diabetes), cardiovascular risk categories and treatment recommendation status (Class I or IIa vs neither) were defined using the 2025 ESC/EAS focused-update framework. Cox models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) adjusted for SCORE2 or for established risk factors. The incremental predictive value of adding the retinal AI risk score to SCORE2 was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation.

Results

Over a 10.0-year median follow-up (914 ASCVD events), the very high retinal AI risk group independently predicted ASCVD (SCORE2-adjusted HR 2.32 vs low risk; p<0.001). Adding the retinal AI risk score to SCORE2 reclassified risk across the ESC/EAS statin-indication boundary (statin-eligibility NRI [net reclassification improvement] 0.012, p<0.001); reclassification was statistically significant but modest (continuous NRI 0.445, p<0.001), without C-index or net-benefit gain. In the statin-indicated subgroup, retinal AI risk groups further stratified risk (SCORE2-adjusted HR 2.16; p<0.001). Statin-not-indicated participants in the high or very high retinal AI risk groups had numerically similar observed 10-year risk to all statin-indicated, untreated participants (p=0.758). There was no evidence of effect modification by clinically detectable retinal disorder (interaction p=0.93). Incremental value was greater in women than men (sex interaction p<0.001).

Conclusion

Adding the retinal AI risk score to SCORE2 produced modest bidirectional risk reclassification across the ESC/EAS statin-indication boundary; these findings warrant prospective validation.Abstract word count: 250 words.

records.title: Automated Structured Reporting of Neurodegenerative Imaging Markers Using Quantitative MRI and Large Language Models.

content.title: Automated Structured Reporting of Neurodegenerative Imaging Markers Using Quantitative MRI and Large Language Models.
content.abstract:
Rationale and objectives

To evaluate the feasibility of a quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-to-structured reporting pipeline that integrates quantitative MRI software with large language models (LLMs) for structured drafting of neurodegenerative imaging markers and generating clinician-facing report conclusions.

Materials and methods

A total of 192 patients with 3D T1 and 2D or 3D FLAIR MRI images from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative database were randomly selected. A deep-learning model generated structured report findings based on nine indices related to brain atrophy, white matter hyperintensities, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) space abnormalities, and compared with neuroradiologist-generated reference reports. Four LLMs (GPT-OSS 20B, MedGemma 4B, Phi-3, and Llama 3.1 8B) generated clinician-facing conclusions from the structured findings. Generated conclusions were evaluated using a five-point Likert scale across four metrics (accuracy, relevance, clarity, and satisfaction). Output errors were assessed across four categories: language, omission, addition, and numeric errors.

Results

Structured report findings demonstrated high accuracy for CSF space analysis (77.6%-97.9%). Performance for ordinal visual scales was lower under strict matching (27.1%-57.8%) but improved with a one-grade tolerance (91.7%-97.4%). Among LLMs, GPT achieved the highest scores across most metrics (median score 5) and exhibited the lowest output error rates. Smaller models (Phi-3 and Llama 3.1 8B) showed overall lower performance, with more language, omission, and addition errors. MedGemma demonstrated intermediate performance, but the highest rate of numeric errors.

Conclusion

Our quantitative MRI-to-structured reporting pipeline, integrating quantitative MRI software with LLM-based conclusion generation, might be feasible for automated structured drafting of neurodegenerative imaging markers.

records.title: Empirical Evaluation of Post Hoc Interpretability Methods for Clinical Trust in Deep Learning Diagnostics.

content.title: Empirical Evaluation of Post Hoc Interpretability Methods for Clinical Trust in Deep Learning Diagnostics.
content.abstract: Background/Objectives: Brain tumor classification from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has been significantly improved through deep learning techniques; however, the lack of interpretability remains a major challenge for clinical adoption. Methods: This study proposes an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)-driven framework for multiclass brain tumor classification using a baseline convolutional neural network (CNN) and four transfer learning models, namely ResNet50, DenseNet121, MobileNetV2, and EfficientNetB0. The models were trained and evaluated on a publicly available brain MRI dataset consisting of glioma, meningioma, and pituitary tumor classes. Their classification performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC), and confusion matrix analysis. To enhance transparency and interpretability, Grad-CAM, LIME, and SHAP were used to visualize and quantify the regions contributing to the classification decisions. Results: Experimental results state that the transfer learning models consistently outperformed the CNN by learning more discriminative feature representations while producing more localized and interpretable explanations. The agreement among Grad-CAM, LIME, and SHAP confirms that the proposed models predominantly relied on tumor regions rather than irrelevant background information, thereby improving the interpretability and reliability of the diagnostic predictions. Conclusions: The proposed framework provides an effective and explainable computer-aided diagnosis system that supports trustworthy deep learning-based brain tumor classification and has the potential for decision-making.

records.title: Accuracy and reproducibility of a large language model in assessing spirometry test acceptability and interpretation: a performance study.

content.title: Accuracy and reproducibility of a large language model in assessing spirometry test acceptability and interpretation: a performance study.
content.abstract:
Background

Spirometry is one of the most used pulmonary function tests for assessing respiratory function and diagnosing ventilatory disorders in clinical practice. Evaluation of test validity and interpretation is typically performed by trained healthcare professionals. The present study aims to evaluate the capability of a publicly available large language model (LLM) to perform quality assurance and interpretations of spirometry tests.

Methods

A total of 150 spirometry tests were retrospectively collected from the pulmonary function laboratories. The spirometry tests were evaluated for acceptability and interpreted by clinicians according to ATS/ERS recommendations as part of standard clinical practice. Subsequently, a publicly available LLM (ChatGPT 5.5) was prompted to evaluate the acceptability and interpret the same spirometry tests according to ATS/ERS criteria. The model interpreted each spirometry test on three separate occasions for assessing reproducibility. Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV), with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), were calculated by comparing LLM assessments with clinician assessments of spirometry test acceptability and interpretation.

Results

For spirometry acceptability evaluation, ChatGPT demonstrated an overall accuracy of 87% (95% CI: 81%-92%), sensitivity of 91% (95% CI: 85%-95%), specificity of 61% (95% CI 39%-80%), PPV of 94% (95% CI: 89%-97%), and NPV of 48(95% CI: 29%-67%) with Cohen's k of 0.46. The spiromteric interpretation agreement with the clinicians reference standard was moderate, with exact agreement of 0.61 (95% CI: 0.54-0.69) while Cohen's Kappa (Unweighted) was 0.47 (95% CI: 0.37-0.56) and Macro F1 score was 0.39 (95% CI: 0.33-0.49). Reproducibility across three independent trials was moderate (Fleiss' κ 0.58). Class-specific interpretation performance varied by category; sensitivity was highest for normal pattern and restrictive defects (0.72), whereas sensitivity for obstructive defects was 0.27. F1-scores were highest for normal and restrictive defects (0.81 and 0.62, respectively).

Conclusion

The current findings suggest that ChatGPT 5.5 has a limited capability, at its current stage of development, to serve as a reliable tool for independent spirometry interpretation in clinical practice. Nevertheless, it may serve as an adjunct to clinical decision-making and educational tools. Prospective controlled studies are needed to confirm these findings.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence in Breast Cancer Diagnosis, Treatment, and Perioperative Management: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Perspectives.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence in Breast Cancer Diagnosis, Treatment, and Perioperative Management: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Perspectives.
content.abstract:
Background

Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy in women globally, accounting for approximately 2.30 million new cases and 666,103 deaths in 2022. Artificial intelligence technologies including machine learning, deep learning, radiomics, and natural language processing have been widely applied across the breast cancer care continuum. However, no systematic review restricted to primary studies with patient-level or image-level data has synthesized evidence spanning all clinical domains simultaneously.

Objectives

To evaluate the performance, methodological quality, and clinical relevance of artificial intelligence primary studies across screening and diagnostic imaging, digital pathology, radiomics, perioperative management, prognostic prediction, and natural language processing in breast cancer.

Methods

PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from January 2015 to May 2026. Eligibility was restricted to original primary research reporting patient-level or image-level data; secondary syntheses were explicitly excluded. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2 and PROBAST. Reporting followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines.

Results

Of 5,275 identified records, 17 primary studies met eligibility criteria. In screening mammography (seven studies; n = 7,540 to 144,231 examinations), deep learning achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 0.876 to 0.939; a randomised trial in 80,033 women demonstrated non-inferiority to double reading with a 44.3% reduction in radiologist workload. In digital pathology (five studies; 270 to 44,732 whole-slide images), deep learning achieved AUC 0.985 to 0.994, exceeding unassisted pathologist performance in lymph node metastasis detection. Magnetic resonance imaging radiomics predicted pathological complete response in HER2-positive breast cancer with AUC 0.80. No breast cancer-specific perioperative primary study met the eligibility criteria. Deep survival networks achieved concordance index 0.626 versus 0.612 for Cox regression in breast cancer cohorts. Natural language processing identified metastatic recurrence in breast cancer clinical records with sensitivity 83% and specificity 73%. Risk of bias was low to moderate for imaging and pathology studies and high for small sample radiomics studies. Density-stratified performance was reported by only two imaging studies, and receptor status prediction from haematoxylin and eosin staining had not been validated as a safe alternative to immunohistochemistry.

Conclusions

Artificial intelligence demonstrated clinically meaningful performance across the five domains with eligible primary studies. Breast cancer-specific perioperative and intensive care primary studies were absent, representing the largest evidence gap. External validation, demographic diversity, and prospective clinical integration evidence remained the most consistently identified limitations. Prediction of molecular receptor status without immunohistochemistry requires rigorous prospective safety validation before it can complement standard testing.

records.title: Is Large Language Model a New Hope for the Global South? A Rapid Bibliometric Synthesis of Artificial Intelligence in Anatomy Education.

content.title: Is Large Language Model a New Hope for the Global South? A Rapid Bibliometric Synthesis of Artificial Intelligence in Anatomy Education.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), especially the recent proliferation of generative Large Language Models (LLMs), is transforming traditional anatomy education by introducing new teaching tools. However, the adoption of these cutting-edge technologies raises questions about global educational equity. It remains unclear whether AI will serve as a digital equalizer or further exacerbate marginalization. This rapid bibliometric synthesis aims to provide a comprehensive, data-driven overview of the "Application of Artificial Intelligence in Anatomy Education" (AAAE). We seek to map the intellectual landscape, detect structural and technological shifts, evaluate the geopolitical disparities, and provide corresponding references. A total of 85 consolidated records were retrieved from Web of Science and Scopus. These data constituted the whole panorama of AAAE. Bibliometrix and CiteSpace were utilized for static and dynamic mapping. A multidisciplinary expert panel validated the thematic clusters using Gwet's AC1 and the Normalized Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI). Publications surged following ChatGPT's release, indicating a shift from specialized computer vision to the application of general-purpose LLMs. While high-income countries maintain leadership, AI could exert a "democratizing effect" on upper-middle-income countries, doubling their odds of publication compared to traditional anatomy. Six research frontiers and three research trajectories were captured, and corresponding implications for future researchers in the global south and north were presented. AAAE could be conducted using a stratified strategy: different expansions of AI technologies for pedagogy; leveraging commercial APIs to bypass infrastructure bottlenecks; and validating open-source models. Global equity critically demands cross-border collaboration and inclusive datasets.

records.title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence-Driven Chatbots in University Level Dental Education: A Systematic Review.

content.title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence-Driven Chatbots in University Level Dental Education: A Systematic Review.
content.abstract:
Background

Artificial intelligence (AI), mainly AI-driven chatbots and large language models (LLMs) is reshaping dental education through adaptive, interactive, and simulation-based learning. While the transition in technology has been rapid, the evidence about the educational effectiveness of these technologies is still very diverse and not entirely directed.

Aim

To analyze the roles, educational effectiveness, and impact of integrating AI-driven chatbots and LLMs in dental education at the university level with a focus on learning outcomes and implementation practices.

Methods

The researchers conducted a thorough search of the electronic databases PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase for articles published from January 2018 to November 2025. This review met the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 criteria and was made up of original research articles on dental studentsand educators who were using AI-based chatbots as interventions. The outcomes measured were knowledge gain, clinical reasoning, diagnostic accuracy, communication skills, and engagement of learners. Due to the differences in the methodologies used the authors opted for a narrative synthesis approach.

Results

Six studies met the eligibility criteria and showed potential benefits of AI-driven chatbots and LLMs for diagnostic reasoning, learning performance, engagement, and individualized feedback although methodological and outcome heterogeneity limited direct comparison.

Conclusion

AI-driven chatbots and LLMs may complement university-level dental education, but their effectiveness and safe implementation require further rigorous evaluation.

records.title: Advancing Cancer Biomarker Discovery Through Multi-Omics, Bioinformatics, and Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review.

content.title: Advancing Cancer Biomarker Discovery Through Multi-Omics, Bioinformatics, and Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review.
content.abstract: The rapid accumulation of multi-omics data provides increasing opportunities for cancer biomarker discovery, but the heterogeneity and high dimensionality of these datasets remain major challenges for data integration and analysis. This review examines the application of bioinformatics and artificial intelligence for multi-omics integration in cancer biomarker research. Common multi-omics data paradigms and integration strategies are discussed, followed by a review of the bioinformatics, machine learning and deep learning approaches applied across 84 included studies. Cross-study comparison showed limited recurrence among the reported biomarkers, with only 15 biomarkers identified in at least four studies. Further assessment of the 13 recurrent protein-coding biomarkers showed significant protein-protein interaction enrichment and functional convergence in cancer-related processes, particularly PI3K/AKT and ERBB2-related signaling. This review also highlights current challenges, including missing data, heterogeneity across datasets, limited independent validation and the interpretability of artificial intelligence models. Future research may benefit from integrating multi-omics data with clinical information, pathological imaging, electronic health records, single-cell multi-omics and radiomics, together with broader datasets and greater use of independent validation to support the translation of multi-omics biomarker findings into clinical applications.

records.title: Experimental Protocols for Developing and Validating Explainable AI Models in Secure Healthcare Diagnostics.

content.title: Experimental Protocols for Developing and Validating Explainable AI Models in Secure Healthcare Diagnostics.
content.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has drastically enhanced healthcare diagnostics with automated disease detection, predictive analytics, and intelligent systems for clinical decision support. Nevertheless, the black-box nature of deep learning models hampers interpretability, clinical trust, and regulatory acceptance and raises concerns about data privacy and cybersecurity. This paper presents comprehensive experimental frameworks for developing and evaluating explainable AI models for secure healthcare diagnostics. The suggested model combines responsible data management, multimodal preprocessing, secure deep learning models, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods, and reproducible validation procedures in a single healthcare diagnostic pipeline. Methods of explaining, such as Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME, and counterfactual analysis, were used to make the models more transparent and understandable for clinicians. At the same time, federated learning and differential privacy methods were used to securely manage highly sensitive patient data. Experimental evaluation has shown 96% classification accuracy, 94% sensitivity, and 95% specificity. These results were consistent in heterogeneous healthcare datasets. Compared to traditional black-box models, the explainability framework not only enhanced the interpretability of the results but also more accurately identified the regions relevant for diagnosis. Moreover, the secure federated learning architecture minimized privacy leakages without sacrificing the predictive performance and remained robust even when exposed to adversarial perturbations. An external evaluation also confirmed the reproducibility and generalizability of the protocols involved. This methodology offers a comprehensive and reliable foundation for deploying AI-powered diagnostics across multiple healthcare domains: radiology, pathology, oncology, cardiology, neurology, and precision medicine.

records.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence for Detecting ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction on 12-Lead Electrocardiograms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

content.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence for Detecting ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction on 12-Lead Electrocardiograms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) may improve electrocardiographic detection of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), but available studies address distinct diagnostic questions. We systematically reviewed studies evaluating AI-based STEMI detection from 12-lead electrocardiograms and separately synthesized AI performance against a clinical reference standard, AI and clinician performance against a clinical reference, and AI agreement with physician electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from January 2010 through March 10, 2025. Bivariate random-effects models generated pooled sensitivity, specificity, and hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (AUC). Twenty-six studies comprising 539,876 ECGs were included. In 20 studies comparing AI with a clinical reference standard, pooled sensitivity was 0.95 (95% confidence interval, 0.91-0.97), specificity 0.95 (0.90-0.98), AUC 0.98 (0.97-0.99), positive likelihood ratio 19.2 (9.3-39.5), and negative likelihood ratio 0.05 (0.03-0.10). In 8 studies reporting both AI and clinician performance against a clinical reference, separate syntheses showed sensitivity of 0.91 (0.86-0.94) for AI versus 0.78 (0.69-0.85) for clinicians, specificity of 0.91 (0.82-0.96) for both, and AUCs of 0.95 and 0.90, respectively. In 7 studies using physician ECG interpretation as the comparator, AI sensitivity was 0.85 (0.70-0.94), specificity 0.99 (0.96-1.00), and AUC 0.98 (0.96-0.99). Sensitivity analyses excluding case-control designs, influential studies, and restricting analyses to deep learning models or raw waveform ECGs produced similar findings.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in the Management of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: A Narrative Review Informed by a Systematic Search.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in the Management of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: A Narrative Review Informed by a Systematic Search.
content.abstract:
Background

Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) remains a leading cause of mortality, and early identification of phenotypes, exacerbation risk, and treatment response remains challenging. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool for improving prediction, classification, and monitoring in COPD. This narrative review, informed by a systematic search, evaluated current AI applications in COPD management.

Methods

The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42024502765) and reported with reference to PRISMA 2020 principles. MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from inception to May 2025. Eligible studies applied Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, or Deep Learning approaches to adult COPD populations for diagnostic, prognostic, monitoring, phenotyping, or disease management purposes. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers, and methodological quality was appraised using design-appropriate tools.

Results

Twenty-two studies met the inclusion criteria. AI demonstrated high discriminative accuracy for COPD diagnosis, exacerbation prediction, and mortality risk (mean Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve [AUROC] = 0.83), although methodological heterogeneity and limited external validation were common. Models integrating multimodal data generally outperformed single-domain approaches. Risk-of-bias assessment identified concerns related to small sample sizes, limited external validation, and incomplete reporting of model development and validation procedures.

Conclusion

Current evidence suggests that AI may support COPD diagnosis, prognostic prediction, and telemonitoring. However, methodological heterogeneity, limited external validation, and inconsistent reporting standards continue to limit clinical translation. Further high-quality, externally validated studies are needed to support implementation in respiratory care.

records.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence for Detecting ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction on 12-Lead Electrocardiograms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

content.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence for Detecting ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction on 12-Lead Electrocardiograms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

records.title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence to Predict Visual Outcome in Patients With Macular Pucker.

content.title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence to Predict Visual Outcome in Patients With Macular Pucker.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To assess the current role of artificial intelligence (AI) to predict postoperative best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) after macular pucker surgery using optical coherence tomography (OCT) data.

Methods

A systematic search was conducted of PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library. Data extraction included study design, demographics, AI model characteristics, and performance metrics. Study quality was assessed using the Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment + Artificial Intelligence tool, and results were synthesized narratively.

Results

Six studies involving 2728 patients (65-71 years) were analyzed. Convolutional neural networks and gradient boosting decision trees were applied to predict postoperative BCVA. The convolutional neural networks ResNet-101 and Inception-ResNet-V2 outperformed human grading, with ResNet-101 achieving the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (0.97). Interpretability techniques identified ectopic inner foveal layers (EIFL) and irregular inner nuclear layer-outer plexiform layer as key predictors.

Conclusions

Deep learning models demonstrate potential in predicting postoperative outcomes from preoperative OCT scans after macular pucker surgery. Advanced architectures such as ResNet-101 and Inception-ResNet-v2 outperform simpler models and expert grading. However, clinical translation depends on model generalizability, interpretability, real-time application, and inclusion of functional data. Future research should emphasize multicenter validation to ensure broader applicability.

records.title: E-MDD: an evidence-guided explainable framework for EEG-based depression recognition.

content.title: E-MDD: an evidence-guided explainable framework for EEG-based depression recognition.
content.abstract:
Introduction

An evidence-guided explainable framework, E-MDD, is developed to integrate high-dimensional EEG representations, neurophysiological biomarkers, and large language models for the recognition of EEG-based depression with concise and evidence-based textual explanations.

Methods

The proposed E-MDD framework consists of three stages: classification, evidence construction, and evidence-guided inference. In the classification stage, two parallel feature extraction branches are employed to extract Electroencephalography latent features and neurophysiological biomarkers, which are subsequently fused and fed into a lightweight multilayer perceptron for the recognition of depression. In the evidence construction stage, the latent feature dimensions of the EEG are aligned with neurophysiological biomarkers, and the model's decision basis is identified to construct structured evidence supporting the classification results. In the evidence-guided inference stage, structured evidence and the proposed evidence-guided prompt are used to guide the large language model in generating concise textual explanations.

Results
